section_summary: This section documents State Department handling of proposed exports to Japan and growing public pressure to restrict shipments of steel, petroleum, aviation gasoline, technical processes, industrial equipment, and other war-related materials. It includes corporate inquiries, export statistics, correspondence with citizens and members of Congress, diplomatic reporting from Tokyo and Chongqing, and discussions of the moral embargo on aviation-related technology. The section concludes with a Chinese Council for Economic Research bulletin arguing that war materials constituted an increasing share of U.S. exports to Japan.

subfiles.title: Telegram to Inland Steel concerning steel exports to Japan
subfiles.to: J. L. Block, Inland Steel Company
subfiles.about: The Department answers an inquiry about exporting semi-finished steel to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Telegram to Inland Steel: no legal objection to exporting steel to Japan; statements on discouraging aeronautical exports will be mailed.

subfiles.title: Inland Steel inquiry about proposed sale to Japan
subfiles.from: J. L. Block, Inland Steel Company
subfiles.about: Inland Steel asks whether the Department objects to negotiations for a large Japanese steel order.
subfiles.summary: Inland Steel's Block reports talks on 50,000-100,000 tons of semi-finished steel for Japan and requests a same-day reply on the Department's wishes.

subfiles.title: Phillips Petroleum report on January deliveries to Mitsui
subfiles.from: K. S. Adams, Phillips Petroleum Company
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, attention Joseph C. Green
subfiles.about: Phillips Petroleum reports blending materials delivered to Mitsui for export to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Phillips Petroleum reports January deliveries to Mitsui: a third of a drum of tetraethyl lead, 19,940 drums of iso-octane and 160 drums of natural petroleum products.

subfiles.title: Request for clarification of Phillips Petroleum report
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: K. S. Adams, Phillips Petroleum Company
subfiles.about: The Department asks Phillips to define its reported naturally occurring petroleum products.
subfiles.summary: Yost acknowledges Phillips's report and asks what products occurring naturally in petroleum means and whether they are blending agents.

subfiles.title: Summary of gasoline exports to Japan and the Soviet Union
subfiles.about: The memorandum summarizes the export figures contained in an attached statistical study.
subfiles.summary: Summary: in 1939 the U.S. shipped about 1.2 million barrels of gasoline to Japan, nearly half aviation grade, plus nearly six million gallons of iso-octane and almost a million pounds of tetraethyl lead.

subfiles.title: Exports of gasoline and blending agents to Japan and the U.S.S.R.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, Division of Controls
subfiles.about: The memorandum compares recent gasoline and blending-agent exports to Japan and the Soviet Union.
subfiles.summary: Tables of 1939-1940 gasoline and blending-agent exports: 562,230 barrels of aviation gasoline, 5,889,398 gallons of iso-octane and 964,952 pounds of tetraethyl lead to Japan, none reported for the USSR.

subfiles.title: Mrs. Taft's appeal to President Roosevelt
subfiles.about: Taft urges action to stop military supplies from reaching Japan.
subfiles.summary: Mrs. Taft, chairing a China relief committee, tells Roosevelt she is gravely concerned about military goods sold to Japan and approves measures to halt them.

subfiles.title: Reply to Mrs. Taft
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges Taft's White House-referred letter about war supplies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost acknowledges Mrs. Taft's February 10 letter, referring her to the Department's February 16 answer on the same subject.

subfiles.title: DuPont inquiry concerning used methanol equipment for Mitsui
subfiles.from: Thomas R. Hanley, E. I. du Pont de Nemours & Company
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Green, Division of Controls
subfiles.about: DuPont asks whether the Department objects to selling used high-pressure equipment to Mitsui for methanol manufacture.
subfiles.summary: DuPont says Mitsui offered to buy second-hand methanol-plant compressors and vessels, without technical knowledge, to save construction time, and asks the Department's view.

subfiles.title: DuPont memorandum on Japanese methanol demand
subfiles.about: The memorandum assesses Japanese methanol consumption and the proposed sale of DuPont equipment.
subfiles.summary: DuPont memorandum: Japan imported methanol mostly from Germany; use in aviation fuel seems unlikely on price, so Japan's interest in used equipment probably aims to save time.

subfiles.title: Department reply on DuPont's methanol-equipment proposal
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: E. I. du Pont de Nemours & Company
subfiles.about: The Department explains how the aviation-gasoline policy applies to DuPont's proposed sale.
subfiles.summary: Green encloses the December 20 policy statement, notes DuPont's own suggestion methanol might go into aircraft fuel, and leaves the company to judge whether the deal violates policy.

subfiles.title: White House referral of student inquiry
subfiles.about: The White House refers a student letter about an embargo on war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Watson sends the enclosed correspondence to the State Department for consideration. He requests that the Department acknowledge it directly.

subfiles.title: Students' request for information on a Japanese embargo
subfiles.about: Two students seek the President's views for a paper on embargoing war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The writers say they are students preparing a term paper on whether the United States should impose an embargo on war materials to Japan. Unsure whether it is proper to ask the President, they request a reply and enclose a stamped envelope.

subfiles.title: Department response to Ewen and Fulkerson
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department explains the legal position and supplies publications concerning exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost states that no existing statute authorizes the proposed embargo and that new legislation would be necessary. He encloses presidential and departmental statements about discouraging aircraft-related exports to countries bombing civilians, along with the National Munitions Control Board's Third Annual Report. The students' stamped envelope is returned.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to memorandum on possible Far Eastern action
subfiles.about: The sheet points to a memorandum proposing possible future action to stop war materials reaching Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a memorandum on early formulation of a Far Eastern program, evaluating possible measures and condemning some courses.

subfiles.title: War Department transmittal of Senator Wiley's inquiry
subfiles.from: Harry H. Woodring, Secretary of War
subfiles.about: Woodring forwards Senator Wiley's request for statistics on war materials sent to Japan, Russia, and Germany.
subfiles.summary: Woodring forwards Senator Wiley's inquiry for W. J. Pettigrew of the American Legion, noting Wiley was told it was referred to State.

subfiles.title: Senator Wiley's referral for W. J. Pettigrew
subfiles.about: Wiley asks that Pettigrew receive information about exports of war materials to three belligerent countries.
subfiles.summary: Senator Wiley's referral asks War to write Pettigrew directly about materials sent to Japan, Russia and Germany since their wars began, with a carbon copy for the senator.

subfiles.title: Reply to W. J. Pettigrew on war-material exports
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department supplies published arms-export data requested through Senator Wiley.
subfiles.summary: Yost sends Pettigrew press releases on licensed and actual arms exports to Japan, the USSR and Germany and the Munitions Control Board's Third Annual Report; other commodity statistics come from Commerce.

subfiles.title: Reply to Senator Wiley
subfiles.about: Hull reports the Department's response to Pettigrew's request.
subfiles.summary: Hull acknowledges Senator Wiley's February 7 communication on war-material exports to Japan, Russia and Germany, enclosing the Pettigrew reply.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment to the Secretary of War
subfiles.to: Harry H. Woodring, Secretary of War
subfiles.about: The State Department acknowledges Woodring's referral of Senator Wiley's inquiry.
subfiles.summary: Note to the Secretary of War recapitulating Wiley's request and enclosing the Department's letters to Pettigrew and Wiley.

subfiles.title: Tokyo telegram on embargo proposals and the Yangtze River
subfiles.about: Grew reports the Japanese foreign minister's comments on a possible American embargo and reopening the Yangtze River.
subfiles.summary: Tokyo telegram: the foreign minister calls Senate postponement of embargo talks temporary, says Japan isn't legally obliged to reopen the Yangtze but the lower river will likely reopen when military conditions permit.

subfiles.title: Herbert C. Jones transmittal of Haynes Foundation resolution
subfiles.about: Jones sends a foundation resolution opposing income derived from oil sales supporting Japan's war.
subfiles.summary: Herbert Jones forwards the Haynes Foundation trustees' resolution, noting the foundation owns 22,000 shares of Union Oil.

subfiles.title: Haynes Foundation resolution on oil sales to Japan
subfiles.from: Board of Trustees, John Randolph Haynes and Dora Haynes Foundation
subfiles.about: The trustees condemn deriving foundation income from petroleum sales that facilitate Japan's war in China.
subfiles.summary: Haynes Foundation resolution: Japan's undeclared war violates treaties, American oil facilitates it, and the trustees feel shame at possibly profiting from suffering in China.

subfiles.title: Note on the surge in January aviation-gasoline exports
subfiles.about: The note calls attention to the unusually high January 1940 aviation-gasoline exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Note calling the figures significant: January 1940 aviation-gasoline exports alone nearly equaled all of Japan's 1939 total.

subfiles.title: Commerce verification of the 468,000-barrel figure
subfiles.about: The note records Department of Commerce confirmation of a Japanese aviation-gasoline export figure.
subfiles.summary: Note: Commerce's Hoppen rechecked the 468,000-barrel figure from export declarations of January 1 to February 6 and found it correct.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on January gasoline exports to Japan
subfiles.to: Charles W. Yost and interested divisions
subfiles.about: Moseley reports preliminary Commerce figures for January gasoline shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Preliminary figures: 468,000 barrels of aviation gasoline to Japan in January 1940 versus 562,230 in all of 1939; regular gasoline 61,434 barrels versus 635,492.

subfiles.title: Treadway transmittal of Oliphant inquiry
subfiles.about: Treadway forwards a constituent's request for information on gasoline shipments to Russia and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Treadway asks State to send R. H. Oliphant directly the requested names of gasoline exporters.

subfiles.title: Oliphant request for names of gasoline suppliers
subfiles.about: Oliphant asks the government to identify companies supplying aviation gasoline to Russia and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Oliphant cites reports that American aviation gasoline enabled Russian and Japanese bombing of civilians and says naming exporters would let consumers pressure them.

subfiles.title: Reply to Oliphant on gasoline exporters and quantities
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department declines to identify exporters but supplies gasoline-export statistics.
subfiles.summary: Yost says regulations bar disclosing individual firms' trade data; the USSR got virtually no aviation gasoline in 1939, Japan got 562,230 barrels and about 468,000 in January 1940.

subfiles.title: Reply to Treadway concerning Oliphant
subfiles.about: Hull informs Treadway that the Department has answered Oliphant's gasoline inquiry.
subfiles.summary: Hull returns Oliphant's letter to Treadway with the Department's response and the December 15 and 20 press releases.

subfiles.title: Letter from a Franklin judge supporting restrictions on war materials
subfiles.from: Unidentified correspondent, Judge's Chambers, Franklin, Pennsylvania
subfiles.about: The writer supports withholding war materials as a means of avoiding foreign entanglements.
subfiles.summary: A Franklin judge favors refusing exports usable for war without singling out Japan, but sees a Japanese embargo as a useful beginning and policy statement.

subfiles.title: Berle routing note to Green
subfiles.about: Berle assigns correspondence concerning aviation-gasoline companies for answer.
subfiles.summary: Berle's note directing Green to prepare a response to Mrs. Vezin's request to identify firms cooperating on aviation-gasoline policy.

subfiles.title: Mrs. Vezin's request for names of cooperating firms
subfiles.about: Vezin asks Berle to identify firms whose cooperation might be praised in a radio broadcast.
subfiles.summary: Mrs. Vezin asks Berle for the names of cooperating firms that Raymond Gram Swing couldn't supply, hoping to use them in a broadcast.

subfiles.title: Swing's reply to Mrs. Vezin
subfiles.about: Swing agrees that the State Department should publish the names of cooperating companies.
subfiles.summary: Swing agrees with Vezin's proposal for disclosure and recommends writing to Adolf Berle, who conferred with the companies.

subfiles.title: Mrs. Vezin's original letter to Swing
subfiles.about: Vezin proposes publicizing and rewarding companies that declined aviation-gasoline work for Russia and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Vezin asks Swing to announce the two companies' names so consumers can support them and boycott firms supplying Japan.

subfiles.title: Department reply to Mrs. Vezin
subfiles.about: The Department declines to identify firms cooperating with its aviation-gasoline policy.
subfiles.summary: Department tells Mrs. Vezin the firms, engineering concerns controlling aviation-gasoline processes, requested confidentiality and cannot be named; all affected companies are cooperating.

subfiles.title: Mrs. Vezin's handwritten follow-up
subfiles.about: A largely illegible handwritten note follows the Department's answer to Mrs. Vezin.
subfiles.summary: Mrs. Vezin's mostly illegible handwritten follow-up on her stationery.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Hull's conversation with the Japanese ambassador
subfiles.about: The sheet points to a memorandum concerning a disputed gasoline-related contract.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Hull's conversation with the Japanese ambassador on an alleged breach of a contract between Japanese agencies and Americans for gasoline exports.

subfiles.title: J. H. Baptist letter advocating economic pressure on Japan
subfiles.about: Baptist asks what trade continues with Japan and urges the withholding of scrap iron and war supplies.
subfiles.summary: J. H. Baptist asks whether scrap iron and war material have kept moving to Japan since January 1939 and argues targeted economic pressure could defeat Japan's conquest of China.

subfiles.title: Referral of Baptist's trade inquiry to Commerce
subfiles.about: The State Department asks Commerce to answer Baptist's questions about trade with Japan.
subfiles.summary: State sends Commerce Baptist's February 27 letter for reply, with a copy of its own acknowledgment.

subfiles.title: State Department acknowledgment to Baptist
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department explains the absence of embargo authority and refers Baptist's trade questions to Commerce.
subfiles.summary: Yost tells Baptist no statute authorizes the embargo he advocates and new legislation would be needed; his letter went to Commerce for an answer on trade.

subfiles.title: K. T. Chen request for export-control publications
subfiles.about: Chen requests printed sources for a paper on government restrictions on arms sales to belligerents.
subfiles.summary: K. T. Chen asks for material on arms controls, including Hull's appeal to aircraft makers concerning Japan, and on neutrality legislation.

subfiles.title: Reply supplying publications to K. T. Chen
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department sends Chen a collection of reports, statutes, statements, and press releases on arms-export controls.
subfiles.summary: Yost encloses the National Munitions Control Board's Third Annual Report, numerous departmental press releases, neutrality materials, and Army and Navy Munitions Board statements. He notes that the fourth annual report is being printed and offers to send it when available.

subfiles.title: James Hoge Ricks letter supporting a firmer Japan policy
subfiles.about: Ricks endorses Representative Satterfield's call to stop exports assisting Japan's war in China.
subfiles.summary: James Ricks cites Satterfield's February 7 address and asks why shipments of munitions and convertible materials should continue making America a partner in Japan's conquest.

subfiles.title: Pacific Northwest Business Association proposal on S.J. Res. 143
subfiles.from: George F. Thorndyke, Pacific Northwest Business Association
subfiles.about: The association proposes amendments giving the executive branch discretion under the Schwellenbach bill.
subfiles.summary: Pacific Northwest Business Association backs S.J. Res. 143, which regulates American conduct, and proposes executive discretion instead of a congressional mandate.

subfiles.title: Chongqing telegram reporting editorial on American Japan policy
subfiles.about: Peck summarizes a Chinese newspaper editorial connecting American policy toward Japan with events in Europe.
subfiles.summary: Chongqing's Central Daily News says most Americans favor economic measures against Japan, embargo consideration may await Welles's talks with Britain, and some fear driving Japan toward Russia.

subfiles.title: Harter transmittal of Mrs. Reuman's letter
subfiles.about: Harter forwards a constituent's concern about American supplies reaching Japan.
subfiles.summary: Harter encloses Mrs. Reuman's letter on American ammunition supplied to Japan against China and asks for an answer and return of the enclosure.

subfiles.title: Mrs. Reuman's inquiry about stopping supplies to Japan
subfiles.about: Reuman asks what measures are being taken to stop American war supplies from reaching Japan.
subfiles.summary: Mrs. Reuman says the U.S. helps supply ammunition and materials for Japan's war on China, urges stopping it, and asks what measures are under way.

subfiles.title: Hull reply to Harter concerning Mrs. Reuman
subfiles.about: Hull provides the Department's standard explanation of the legal position on an embargo.
subfiles.summary: Hull says the Department appreciates the referral and explains that no current statute authorizes the embargo advocated by Reuman. New legislation would be necessary, and several related bills had been introduced. Reuman's original letter is returned as requested.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Morito Morishima about the Japan Gasoline Company
subfiles.about: Morishima seeks an exception to the moral embargo for a contract between Universal Oil Products and the Japan Gasoline Company.
subfiles.summary: Morishima says the Japan Gasoline Company faces financial difficulty since American policy blocks its technical-process contract and asks partial performance; Hamilton says no case-by-case exceptions are made.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Tokyo enclosing Morishima conversation
subfiles.about: The Department transmits the memorandum of its discussion with Morishima to the embassy in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Instruction to Tokyo enclosing the February 16 memorandum on the Universal Oil Products-Japan Gasoline Company contract for the ambassador.

subfiles.title: Baldwin Locomotive inquiry about an armor-plate press
subfiles.about: Baldwin representatives ask whether selling Japan a press for naval armor-plate manufacture conflicts with law or policy.
subfiles.summary: Baldwin Locomotive asks about a $1 million armor-plate press for Japan; Yost says no law or the moral embargo prohibits it, so the decision is Baldwin's.

subfiles.title: Policy statement sent to A. O. Smith Corporation
subfiles.from: Department of State, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department sends the company its policy statement on aviation-gasoline technology.
subfiles.summary: Form letter sending A. O. Smith Corporation the December 20, 1939 statement on delivering aviation-gasoline plants, rights and technical information.

subfiles.title: Policy statement sent to Petro-Chem Development Company
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department sends Petro-Chem its policy statement on aviation-gasoline technology.
subfiles.summary: Form letter sending Petro-Chem Development Company the December 20, 1939 aviation-gasoline technology policy statement.

subfiles.title: Policy statement sent to Asano Bussan Company
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department sends Asano Bussan its statement restricting aviation-gasoline technology transfers.
subfiles.summary: Form letter sending Asano Bussan Company the December 20, 1939 policy statement on aviation-gasoline plants and information.

subfiles.title: Policy statement sent to Okura & Company
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department sends Okura its statement on transfers of aviation-gasoline production technology.
subfiles.summary: Form letter sending Okura & Company the December 20, 1939 policy statement on aviation-gasoline plants and information.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to data on war-material exports to Japan
subfiles.about: The sheet identifies another file containing data on war-material exports to Japan from July 1937 through January 1940.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a memorandum submitting export data on war-material exports to Japan, file 893.24/697.

subfiles.title: Sale of War Materials by the United States to Japan, January–August 1939
subfiles.about: The bulletin compares U.S. exports considered essential for Japanese war purposes during the first eight months of 1937, 1938, and 1939.
subfiles.summary: Detailed tables cover petroleum, scrap iron and steel, metals, machinery, vehicles, aircraft, ammunition, and other commodities. The bulletin calculates $96.6 million in war-material exports during January–August 1939 and argues that such goods rose to 71.28 percent of all U.S. exports to Japan, despite an overall decline in trade. Petroleum ranked first by value, followed by scrap iron and steel, metal-working machinery, and copper; the discussion emphasizes rising gasoline shipments and Japan's dependence on American scrap. The bulletin continues beyond page 240.
